#5265. XRP News: Thanksgiving Rally or December 1 Supply Shock?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP has a history of making Thanksgiving interesting, old news for some. In 2024, Ripple surged nearly 49% in the three days following the holiday. Last year, it went nowhere. Now, XRP is heading into another Thanksgiving with $1 in sight and Ripple’s 1 billion-token escrow unlock looming on December 1.

The timing puts bulls in a tight spot. XRP is recovering from a November sell-off, but the rebound has yet to clear major resistance. A holiday rally could give buyers some breathing room before next week’s token release puts supply back in the spotlight.

The 2024 Thanksgiving weekend was anything but quiet for XRP. The token closed November 28 at $1.54, climbed to $1.80 the following day, and reached $2.29 by December 1. That was a gain of nearly 49% from Thanksgiving’s close.

The rally had fuel beyond holiday trading as Donald Trump’s election victory revived hopes for a friendlier crypto regulatory environment, while XRP was breaking out after years of being held back by its SEC lawsuit. Buyers were chasing momentum, and the long weekend did little to slow them down.

Last year’s price action was considerably less exciting. XRP closed Thanksgiving on November 27, 2025, near $2.20, then drifted around $2.16 over the following days. The market offered no repeat of the explosive move seen a year earlier.

That history makes this year’s comparison interesting, but the conditions are different. XRP is entering Thanksgiving after a painful November decline.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

XRP’s recovery toward $0.95 has brought the psychological $1 level back into play. Buyers have been defending the area below $0.90, preventing another immediate breakdown and giving the short-term chart some breathing room.

But the problem is overhead resistance, as XRP must first push through $0.96–$0.98 before $1 becomes a realistic breakout target. That zone has become the immediate test for buyers. A clean move through it could attract momentum traders and open the path toward $1.02 and $1.08.

The $1 mark matters because XRP has spent November losing ground. Reclaiming it would put the token back above an important psychological threshold and give bulls something concrete to work with.

Failure to break resistance could leave the rebound looking like another dead-cat bounce. XRP’s recent low around $0.89 remains the level to watch. Losing it would put $0.86 back on the radar and risk undoing the recovery.

For now, the chart is caught between an improving short-term bounce and a damaged larger trend. Bulls have a chance, but they need to turn that chance into a breakout.

The next complication arrives Monday, with Ripple’s scheduled escrow contracts. It will release 1 billion XRP, renewing concerns about supply just as the token tries to recover from bad geopolitical news.

The billion-token headline sounds worse than Ripple’s typical net release. Over the past year, the company has re-escrowed around 70% of monthly unlocks, leaving around 300 million XRP outside escrow on average. The market will be watching whether December follows the same pattern.

The full 1 billion XRP unlock is not equivalent to 1 billion tokens hitting exchanges for sale. What Ripple re-locks, retains, or moves afterward will determine how much circulating supply actually changes.

What does it need? XRP cannot afford to enter Monday with a failed breakout and weakening support. If buyers reclaim $1 before the unlock, sentiment could shift in their favor. If XRP remains pinned below resistance, the escrow event gives nervous traders another reason to stay cautious.

Thanksgiving delivered XRP a spectacular rally in 2024. This year, bulls need more than a holiday repeat; they need the $1 back.

#5264. Flop Labs Pushes Back Testnet Launch Amid Final Preparations

Flop Labs has announced a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any plans to move the testnet launch to another day.

Flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

#5263. Trezor Tells Crypto Users Never to Enter Wallet Backups on Phones Amid Theft Probe

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency users following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website."

According to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

According to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

The device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim says they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

On November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is currently no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

Trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are currently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

@OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and shows no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the company and showed no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an important security warning: users should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

#5262. Solana Validators Can Now Stop Block Processing

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

This PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or issues with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

This PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

This is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's important not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

For everyday users, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

#5260. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

The Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist Mike McGlone declared on Sunday that “the everything bubble is bursting,” arguing that broad declines across major assets are already under way after years of aggressive money creation.

In the first half of his post, McGlone said the Bitcoin and crypto bear market since October 2025 “may be a guide of what to expect in most markets, particularly the US stock market, gold, metals, commodities and US Treasury bond yields; they’re all going down. It’s simply overdue reversion.”

He expects sharp short-covering rallies that “typically gotta keep false hope alive to feed the bear,” comparing many cryptocurrencies to the collapse of NFTs and warning that tokens tracking nothing could approach zero. Bitcoin, he added, may find a “good gravity-pull pivot” near $10,000 to clear speculative excess.

In the second half of his post, McGlone argued that the strong annual gains previously seen in Bitcoin, natural gas, gold, silver and other commodities would reverse and spread weakness into the broader stock market, potentially leaving the S&P 500 with its third annual decline since 2009.

He anticipates significant drawdowns that began from early October highs, lower prices for crude oil and copper, a shift by the Federal Reserve toward easing, and a normal post-inflation period of deflation as US housing peaks. Elevated mortgage rates and Treasury yields, he said, will later be viewed as an opportunity for investors, with the year more likely to finish in volatility than calm.

Traders on Polymarket now see about a 97% chance that the Fed raises rates at its December 8-9 meeting. That would be the Fed’s second hike of 2026, after September’s.

Stocks fell hard. The Nasdaq dropped as much as 4.4% in the first hour of trading, led by Nvidia, and bitcoin slid to $57,300. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.82% as investors moved into bonds.

So what does a December hike mean for crypto?

The Bureau of Economic Analysis report gave the Fed little reason to wait:

Strong incomes and sticky prices are the mix that worries a central bank. Polymarket’s December market puts a quarter-point hike at 94% and a half-point hike at 2.6%, with $58 million traded on it.

The year has turned around for the Fed. In January, two officials voted for a rate cut. By September, under Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over in May, the Fed raised its target range by 0.25 points to 3.75%-4%. In October, it held, but two officials wanted another hike. A December move would lift the range to 4%-4.25%.

The inflation report landed on a market already shaken by the AI sell-off. Early on Wednesday, CNBC’s market blog showed the Nasdaq down 4.4%, the S&P 500 down 3.1% and the Dow down more than 1,000 points.

Higher rates hit expensive growth stocks hardest, because they make future profits worth less today. Bitcoin, which has traded with tech stocks all autumn, fell more than 4% in 24 hours.

A hike sounds like bad news for crypto. This year’s data tell a more mixed story. We measured bitcoin’s move in the week after each 2026 Fed rate decision, from the open on decision day to the close seven days later.

The pattern fits an old market saying: sell the rumor, buy the news. By the time the Fed acts, a hike is often already in the price. Seven meetings and one hike is a small sample, so treat it as a clue, not a rule.

The December Fed rate decision is now about the size of the hike and what officials signal for 2027. Until then, $57,800 is the line to watch for bitcoin.

On Tuesday morning, the crypto market gave back almost all of the gains it made after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO on Monday. According to CoinMarketCap data, the price of Bitcoin stood at around $60,000 on Tuesday morning, and on Monday evening, Bitcoin was trading as high as $64,372. XRP was back at $0.93 on Tuesday morning after the cryptocurrency reached $1.026 on Monday.

The price of Ethereum was between $1,680 and $1,695 on Tuesday morning, according to CoinMarketCap. In addition, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index stood at 10 on Tuesday, and the index showed extreme fear in the market.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had $569.7 million in net outflows on Monday, Nov. 23, SoSoValue data shows. Spot XRP ETFs in the U.S. also saw outflows on Monday, and the total amount of these outflows was $2.5 million.

On Monday, Nvidia's board voted to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO after input from senior levels of the U.S. government, according to the company's press release. Nvidia shares closed 31.5% higher at $165.05, and the company added $954.3 billion in market value in one session. That is more than twice the previous one-day record of $450 billion that Microsoft set in July.

The S&P 500 gained 4.73% on Monday, and the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.86%. Bitcoin followed the rally and rose to $64,372 on Monday evening, and XRP reached $1.026.

Nvidia shares were down 4.1% at $158.03 in premarket trading on Tuesday, and Nasdaq 100 futures lost 1.62% on Tuesday morning. The VIX rose 8.72% to 28.93 at the same time.

Anthropic shares traded below the $83 IPO price on Tuesday. Earlier, all seven co-founders of the AI company filed to sell a combined $1.96 billion worth of Anthropic stock, or about $280 million each, and there was also news about internal safety problems at Anthropic.

According to CoinGlass data, 146,356 traders were liquidated over the past 24 hours, and the total amount of liquidations reached $875 million.

Short sellers were hit first during Monday's rally, and short positions accounted for $473 million of the total. The largest single liquidation was a $17.83 million BTC-USD position on Hyperliquid. On Tuesday morning, it was the turn of long positions. Over the past 12 hours, longs accounted for $168.85 million out of $207.37 million in liquidations.

Bitcoin dropped as low as $59,366 and was trading at around $60,300 on Tuesday morning, down 1.5% over 24 hours. Bitcoin liquidations amounted to $372.68 million. In addition, open interest in Bitcoin futures rose 1.31% to $39.49 billion as the price was going down.

XRP followed Bitcoin and fell from $1.026 to $0.9238 before it stabilized at around $0.93. XRP liquidations reached $14.05 million over 24 hours, and 3,350 traders were affected. The Coinbase premium for XRP was -0.13%, and the premium for XRP in South Korea was 1.56%.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes also commented on the Nvidia rally. According to Hayes, Nvidia's rise is the worst-case scenario for crypto portfolios. Hayes said that crypto needs a crash in U.S. stocks that would force the Fed to start printing money again.

The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a forfeiture complaint against more than $1.1 billion in USDC stablecoins. The funds were stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers on Oct. 29, and Circle helped the authorities with the case. According to the Department of Justice, North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance in the attack. Earlier in November, the department said that U.S. authorities and private companies had frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds.

The Ethereum Foundation also addressed the threat of artificial intelligence. According to the foundation, AI is a more urgent threat to the network than quantum computers. In a blog post, the EF developers said that AI finds vulnerabilities in code faster than auditors can check them, and they also said that AI could break mathematical algorithms that have been used for decades.

EF researcher Justin Drake also spoke about Ethereum's move to hash-based cryptography at Devcon 8 in Mumbai. Drake said that he hoped to complete the transition by December 2028. Earlier, the Ethereum Foundation set December 2029 as the deadline for quantum resistance in its roadmap.

There was other news from regulators and banks as well:

According to Grayscale, the current bear market for Bitcoin has lasted 411 days, and it is the longest one in history. Still, Grayscale called it the mildest one. Bitcoin fell 56% from its October 2025 peak of $124,824 to last week's low of $55,254, according to Grayscale.

Galaxy Research put the drawdown at 53%. According to Galaxy, Bitcoin lost 85%, 84% and 77% in the bear markets of 2013–2015, 2017–2018 and 2021–2022, respectively.

The market capitalization of altcoins excluding Bitcoin and Ethereum dropped to $630.71 billion on Tuesday.

According to CoinGlass data, large buy orders for Bitcoin on OKX and Binance were placed between $59,137 and $59,366 on Tuesday, and $30.3 million worth of long positions could be liquidated in the same range. A large sell order for Bitcoin was placed on Hyperliquid at $60,682, and $64.4 million worth of short positions could be liquidated near $63,996.

The max pain price for Bitcoin options expiring on Nov. 25 stood at $61,000, and the notional value of these options was $642.3 million.

For XRP, liquidations data shows a buy order on Gate at $0.9240 and $577,200 worth of long positions that could be liquidated at $0.9187. Sell orders for XRP on Gate and Hyperliquid were placed between $0.9340 and $0.9444, and $1.4 million worth of short positions could be liquidated at $0.9887.

Two-year U.S. inflation swaps fell to 2.09% ahead of the PCE report, the lowest level for the swaps since September 2024.

In a new announcement, Binance crypto exchange said it will perform wallet maintenance on November 25, 2026 at 06:00 (UTC). To support the wallet maintenance, Binance stated that withdrawals for all networks will be suspended beginning on November 25, 2026 at 06:00 (UTC). The recovery is estimated to take about 60 minutes.

The trading of tokens on Binance will not be impacted during the wallet maintenance. The exchange did not announce a corresponding suspension of deposits in the notice. Thus, the temporary suspension specifically concerns withdrawals across all networks.

In its notice, Binance said that withdrawal services will be resumed when the network is deemed to be stable and that no further announcement may be made.

Those looking to transfer funds should make their withdrawals before the wallet maintenance is set to begin to avoid delays and possible loss of funds.

Wallet maintenance refers to a standard operational process that supports blockchain updates, system improvements, and fund security.

This comes weeks after Binance suffered an historic hack with $6.3 billion in assets affected. Binance has since completed coverage of assets impacted in the security incident and published a new Proof of Reserves snapshot.

In a recent development, Binance stated it has engaged leading security firms Mandiant, SlowMist and Verichains for independent reviews of its security procedures.

These reviews, the exchange said, will validate its current security infrastructure, assess its security posture going forward, and help strengthen the protections expected from the crypto platform.

Binance also stated that it was coordinating closely with the U.S. Department of Justice, as well as with industry partners who have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the security incident in late October 2026.  The collaboration is necessary throughout the asset forfeiture process, with the goal of supporting the return of affected funds as efficiently as possible.

In separate news, Binance said it has integrated the Cboe Global Indices Feed into its platform, app and Binance AI, giving users access to real-time traditional market data. The initial rollout covers three of the world's most widely followed U.S. equity benchmarks, with more benchmark data to follow: S&P 500 Index, Dow Jones Industrial Average, Nasdaq-100.

Ripple's U.S. dollar stablecoin Ripple USD (RLUSD) has overtaken Gram (GRAM), the token previously known as Toncoin, in the CoinMarketCap ranking of cryptocurrencies by market capitalization.

According to CoinMarketCap data, RLUSD had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and ranked No. 26, and Gram dropped to No. 27 with a market capitalization of $2.79 billion.

Gram fell below $1 and was trading at around $0.97 on Tuesday, down about 6% over the past seven days, according to CoinMarketCap. The 24-hour trading volume of Gram stood at around $47 million, and RLUSD had about $368 million in trading volume over the same period.

World Liberty Financial USD (USD1) also had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and was one spot higher, at No. 25. Among stablecoins, Tether (USDT) and USDC still lead the list with $174.64 billion and $69.22 billion, respectively.

In late July, the market value of RLUSD was about $1.5 billion, according to RWA.xyz data. On Aug. 25, Ripple said that RLUSD had crossed $2 billion in market capitalization, with close to $1 billion of the supply issued on the XRP Ledger. By mid-September, RLUSD supply stood at $2.44 billion.

In late October, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave Ripple approval for Ripple National Trust Bank. A day later, on Oct. 27, Moody's Ratings assigned RLUSD an A2 long-term deposit rating and a P-1 short-term deposit rating. RLUSD is issued by Ripple subsidiary Standard Custody & Trust Company. Also in late October, RLUSD became available on Coinbase and Robinhood.

The Open Network renamed its token from Toncoin to Gram in June 2026. On July 21, Telegram founder Pavel Durov announced a native non-custodial Gram wallet for every Telegram app. "This summer will see the largest rollout of a non-custodial crypto wallet in human history. Instant zero-fee crypto transactions for over a billion users are about to become reality," Durov wrote.

This week, Telegram published the terms of service for Gram Wallet. According to the terms, the wallet is operated by RAZOR UNIVERSAL CORP., a Panamanian company, and Telegram provides the apps through which users access it. "Telegram does not operate Gram Wallet, does not hold your keys or assets, and is not a party to these Terms," the document says.

The terms also say that "neither we nor Telegram can freeze, seize, move, recover or reverse your assets." At the same time, according to the terms, "anyone who visits your Telegram profile may be able to see your associated Gram Wallet address," as well as the total balance of the wallet. Access to the wallet "may be restricted or unavailable in certain regions or to certain users," the document says.

#5254. Will Crypto Recover? Does BTC Reclaiming $60K Offer Hope?

Will Crypto Recover? Everyone is wondering this right now after the entire crypto market surged around +2% overnight. An Optimistic Look After Bitcoin’s Rebound Above $ 60,000.

The cryptocurrency market delivered a welcome dose of relief over the past 24 hours. Bitcoin reclaimed the $60,000 level, rising roughly 2.5–3.5% to trade between $60,400 and $60,800, while the broader market advanced in tandem.

Ethereum climbed to the $1,690–$1,710 range, XRP advanced toward $0.95–$0.96, and total crypto market capitalization pushed higher toward $2.15–$2.16 trillion.

After weeks of heavy selling and extreme fear, the bounce has sparked renewed discussion about whether this could mark the early stages of a more sustained recovery heading into 2027.

Prices became deeply oversold after Bitcoin’s slide toward the mid-$50,000s earlier in the week, with short-term RSI readings hitting extreme lows that historically attract dip-buyers and mean-reversion algorithms.

Forced short covering amplified the move higher as leveraged bearish positions were liquidated. A concurrent recovery in technology and AI-related equities improved broader risk appetite, and crypto’s high correlation with those sectors helped lift digital assets.

Thin holiday trading volumes around Thanksgiving also magnified price swings. On the policy front, progress on a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill that cleared a House committee provided a modest sentiment boost, reminding participants that longer-term institutional and governmental interest has not vanished.

XRP's Long Wait Could Finally Pay OffTokentus Investment CEO Oliver Michel expects $XRP (@XRP) to rally around February or March.He believes the next bullish phase could bring a major price peak. Michel says he could sell all his XRP holdings at that point.He previously… pic.twitter.com/MTq8iBJan3

Its ability to hold above $60,000 after testing lower support is constructive in the short term. While November has seen record ETF outflows exceeding $5 billion, the latest rebound shows that demand can still emerge at discounted levels.

Ethereum has tracked Bitcoin closely, benefiting from improved risk appetite and its role as the leading smart-contract platform. XRP has shown relative strength in the bounce, gaining around 3–4.5% as traders watch for potential follow-through if it can challenge higher levels near $1.

Looking further ahead, the case for recovery into 2027 rests on several structural factors. Crypto markets have repeatedly shown resilience after deep corrections, often bottoming when sentiment reaches extreme fear, as in recent weeks.

Persistent institutional infrastructure, including spot ETFs, corporate treasury strategies, and ongoing development in tokenization and payments, provides a foundation for renewed capital inflows once macroeconomic conditions stabilize.

Policy developments, such as clearer regulatory frameworks or expanded strategic reserve discussions, could act as positive catalysts. One example is the US Bitcoin Strategic Reserve Bill, which was recently cleared and is now headed to the House.

Historically, post-halving cycles and periods of oversold conditions have preceded stronger multi-month advances, and many participants view current levels as a potential accumulation zone rather than the start of a prolonged bear market.

Of course, risks remain. Continued heavy ETF outflows, sticky inflation data, or a shift toward tighter monetary policy could pressure prices again.

Yet the speed with which buyers stepped in during the latest dip suggests underlying demand remains. If Bitcoin can build a series of higher lows and reclaim key moving averages, confidence is likely to improve across the board.

In short, while one rebound does not confirm a full bull market, the past 24 hours offer encouraging signs that selling pressure may be exhausting itself.

Combined with oversold technicals, short covering, supportive equity moves, and longer-term policy and institutional tailwinds, crypto has a credible path to recover more meaningfully through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.

For now, the market has shown it can still bounce, and that alone is a constructive first step. However, green weekly closes across the major cap tokens are the next step in seeing whether this rally has any legs.

#5253. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. XRP has completed a short-term golden cross against Bitcoin, giving bulls a fresh technical signal as the cryptocurrency eyes a retest of $1.

The 50 MA rose above the 200 MA on the 3-hour chart, completing a golden cross, as XRP saw relative outperformance against Bitcoin. The timing of the golden cross remains surprising given the current selling in the market.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 5.83% in the last 24 hours to $0.923, giving back most of a rally that sharply took it past $1 after Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia.

On Monday, Nvidia shocked the markets with the surprise announcement of Jensen Huang returning as the CEO of the popular tech and AI company. For crypto traders, the initial response looked extremely encouraging as most tokens sharply rose. However, the rebound began fading, with most cryptocurrencies seeing visible losses in an ongoing selloff in the early Tuesday session.

Bitcoin was down 5.23% in the last 24 hours to $60,298, with total liquidations across the crypto market reaching $596 million.

The $1 price point remains significant for XRP as it is slightly above the lower boundary of the channel in which XRP traded in recent months.

XRP failed to break above the $1.55 resistance at the top of the channel and completed a full reversal toward the channel’s lower boundary at $0.99. XRP broke below this key support level in the past week, cascading to a low of $0.86, last seen in November 2024.

This drop also coincided with a death cross on the daily chart of its USD pairing, the first such occurrence in 2026. For the bearish outlook to weaken, XRP would need to reclaim $0.99 as support.

Although Bitcoin has recently reclaimed the $60,000 price mark after seeing a sudden shift in market sentiments that triggered increases of over 6% in its price during the last day, momentum has slowed again, further stretching the prolonged volatility seen over the past months.

With the Bitcoin bear market still persisting, Grayscale has sparked discussions across the crypto market after drawing attention toward a major bearish milestone for the asset.

While this marks an historic milestone in the Bitcoin bear market, Grayscale further disclosed an interesting twist that makes the current bear market pretty different from previous times.

All through the current bear market, Bitcoin has only posted a price decrease 56%, suggesting that it has suffered considerably smaller losses than several previous bear markets.

This means that even though Bitcoin has spent more than a year in a bear market, its decline has not been as severe as those seen in earlier cycles.

To back the data, Grayscale showed charts comparing Bitcoin's performance across historical bear markets that ended in June 2011, December 2013, December 2017, November 2021, and the ongoing October 2025 cycle.

While the 2011, 2017 and 2021 bear cycles suffered massive losses, especially during the former when its indexed performance fell below 10, the current 2025 bear market broke historical pattern by enduring a longer period yet a comparatively modest decline in Bitcoin’s price.

#5248. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5247. Saylor Spots New Role for Bitcoin

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees new ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.

According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S. derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses.

‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov. 23.

As per the guidance, these companies must maintain sufficient financial resources to cover their operating costs for at least a year.

As clarified by CFTC staff, Bitcoin and Ether can be used to meet this requirement (as well as payment stablecoins). The advisory also provides guidance on how staff interpret the current rules. It also applies to swap execution facilities (SEFs), which are platforms where counterparties trade swaps.

Bitcoin holdings worth $10 million could count for $8 million toward the annual requirement, based on the minimum 20% discount that CFTC staff said they would accept. This provides some flexibility in case Bitcoin's price falls. The discount is also called a haircut.

For Ether, the same minimum 20% haircut applies. For payment stablecoins, the haircut is 2%.

This provides some incentive for an exchange to actually hold BTC. Exchanges could hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets and use some of its value to satisfy this reserve requirement. There would be no need to sell it for USD first.

However, a futures exchange still needs to have sufficient unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover its operating costs for at least six months. Bitcoin, Ether and even payment stablecoins do not fall into this category.

The same six-month liquidity requirement applies to clearinghouses. Additionally, they need to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover a default by a clearing member.

CFTC staff also noted a potential downside for exchanges holding crypto reserves. During a market slump, there's a risk that an exchange's operating losses might rise. At the same time, the value of the Bitcoin it holds to cover those losses might fall.

So this possibility should be considered before an exchange decides whether to use Bitcoin to meet its financial resource requirements.

Each account trading on the XRP Ledger's decentralized exchange moved an average of 4,328 XRP a day in the third quarter of 2026, up 437% from 805 XRP in the same quarter a year earlier, according to a report that XRP treasury company Evernorth released on Tuesday.

According to Evernorth, the average swap on the XRP Ledger reached 35 XRP in the third quarter, up from 19 XRP in the second quarter and under 6 XRP a year earlier. "The growth came from bigger trades, not more of them," the company wrote in the report.

At the same time, the number of accounts trading on the XRP Ledger's order book fell to 1,042 a day in the third quarter of 2026 from 2,027 a day in the third quarter of 2025. The number stood at 1,203 in the fourth quarter of 2025, 1,324 in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,125 in the second quarter, according to the report.

Order-book volume on the XRP Ledger rose to 4.51 million XRP a day in the third quarter from 1.63 million XRP a day a year earlier, Evernorth data shows.

In total, 5.16 million XRP a day was traded on the XRP Ledger's exchange in the third quarter, and the figure was up 96% year over year, according to Evernorth.

Measured in U.S. dollars, exchange volume on the XRP Ledger fell 15% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the report.

Evernorth also compared the XRP Ledger with Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche and Polygon. Across these seven networks, exchange volume in dollars fell 42% over the same period, the report shows.

XRP was trading at around $0.93 on Tuesday morning after reaching as high as $1.026 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap.

The report also shows that the average balance of Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin on the XRP Ledger reached $937 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from $539 million in the second quarter. By the end of the quarter, the RLUSD balance on the XRP Ledger stood at $1.15 billion, compared with $670 million at the end of the second quarter, and the number of RLUSD holders on the network rose to 67,449 from 45,620.

According to Evernorth, the XRP Ledger's average share of RLUSD reached 48.5% in the third quarter, up from 34% in the second quarter. Still, Ethereum finished the quarter with more RLUSD than the XRP Ledger. Evernorth noted that on Ethereum, RLUSD "can already be lent," and that on the XRP Ledger, "native lending is in validator voting."

As of Nov. 20, the Lending Protocol amendment had 24 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. The amendment needs 29 votes, held for 14 days, to activate.

Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9, and its shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN on Oct. 12. The company entered the public markets holding approximately 473 million XRP, according to its press release.

Evernorth announced the deal in October 2025, with investments from SBI, Ripple, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

#5245. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

#5243. LINK, AAVE and UNI Now Supported by Fidelity

Fidelity Investments now supports three new cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where users can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

On July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the company introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it launched Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible users can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

Monday brought a sharp rebound across crypto markets after Bitcoin's weekend crash toward $55,000.

Meanwhile, U.S. authorities took action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency linked to the October Binance hack.

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture action on Nov. 23 seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in USDC allegedly stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers.

The assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government. The latest filing represents another step toward recovering funds following the Oct. 29 attack, which reportedly resulted in more than $6 billion in stolen cryptocurrency.

The DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

U.S. authorities said they had helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in cryptocurrency since the theft. The case highlights the role of cooperation between law enforcement agencies and crypto companies in tracking and recovering stolen digital assets.

Strategy purchased another 457 BTC for approximately $29.6 million, according to a Nov. 23 report based on the company's SEC filing.

The latest acquisition was made at an average price of $64,898 per Bitcoin, bringing Strategy's holdings to approximately 851,305 BTC. The company has spent around $64.23 billion accumulating Bitcoin at an average purchase price of $75,446.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

#5240. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

#5239. End of Crypto Trading? How AI Replaces Ones Who Pumped Bitcoin (BTC)

The “pump” trade could be taken to new extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing issues with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a new occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

Are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Institutions are (and will continue to be) an important source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

Institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

The future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

#5238. Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Cleared for December 15 Test: Will ETH Rally Like After Pectra?
