#5211. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery plan has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

SlowMist's finding is precise: the withdrawal function released assets without independently verifying the actual event on the source chain. A signature confirmed that the signer approved a message. It did not confirm that the message matched a deposit that existed, that was still unused, and that involved the same recipient, token and amount.The replay angle deserves attention, even though SlowMist's summary only implies it. A bridge normally marks each source event as consumed, keyed to something fixed like the source chain, transaction hash and log index, so it can be paid out once. If replay protection keys on the contents of the receipt instead, changing the recipient, token or amount produces a receipt the contract has never seen. Five edited receipts against one deposit would then look like five fresh claims. That is one plausible way the pieces fit together, not a finding the researchers have published.Bridge history offers parallels. In 2022, Wormhole lost about $325 million when an attacker got a forged message past its signature verification, and Nomad lost about $190 million after a misconfiguration let nearly any message pass as valid. The Ankr case is smaller, but it shares the same root: the verification step accepted something it shouldn't have.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

#5209. Ripple’s $900 Million Revenue Target Raises Questions About XRP’s Stagnant Price

Ripple’s growing business operations and ambitious $900 million revenue target are drawing attention to the disconnect between the company’s commercial expansion and XRP’s price performance.

Despite increasing its presence in institutional payments, corporate treasury management, stablecoin services and digital asset custody, Ripple has yet to see comparable strength in its native cryptocurrency.

During a November 19 interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse addressed the disconnect, attributing XRP’s relative weakness to broader cryptocurrency market conditions and shifting investor demand.

He explained that digital assets remain sensitive to changes in market sentiment, with competing investment opportunities potentially drawing capital away from cryptocurrencies.

The executive pointed to SpaceX’s anticipated public listing and Anthropic’s stock market debut as developments that may have attracted capital away from liquid cryptocurrency holdings. He noted that selling pressure across the crypto market coincided with these events, although he provided no figures confirming direct capital movements from XRP into either company.

Despite the market downturn, Garlinghouse described Ripple’s business performance as particularly strong.

“Ripple has had a phenomenal year despite the fact that the market around crypto has come way down,” he said.

The company has been expanding beyond cross-border payments, targeting institutional brokerage, stablecoins, custody and corporate treasury services. The boss believes blockchain technology can make financial transactions faster and cheaper, creating opportunities across insurance, payments and the tokenization of traditional assets.

However, Ripple’s commercial success does not automatically increase XRP’s value. The company is privately held, and owning its cryptocurrency does not give investors an ownership stake in its business or a direct claim to its revenue. The company also uses stablecoins and traditional payment infrastructure where appropriate, meaning not every service it provides necessarily requires XRP.

Integration of artificial intelligence into corporate treasury services is another factor contributing to Ripple’s expansion. During the interview, Garlinghouse explained that AI-powered tools can help businesses monitor liquidity across different markets, identify currency shortages, and prepare for upcoming financial obligations.

For instance, the technology can alert corporate treasury managers when available funds in a particular currency may be insufficient to cover upcoming payroll expenses.

Garlinghouse said these capabilities are already generating demand for the company’s treasury products.

“Adding intelligence and using AI agents to make your job easier is something we are doing today and it has driven a ton of demand around our corporate treasury solution,” he explained.

Meanwhile, Garlinghouse expects cryptocurrency performance to become increasingly divided as investors pay greater attention to the practical applications and adoption of individual digital assets. This could mean that projects with stronger real-world utility attract more interest than those relying primarily on market speculation.

He compared the current enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence with the early internet era, acknowledging that investor expectations can sometimes exceed technological progress.

“Some days that hype gets ahead of reality,” he said, arguing that expectations and actual results eventually reach equilibrium.

That said, Ripple’s expanding operations will need to generate stronger demand for XRP itself before the company’s commercial success can translate into sustained price appreciation. Whether increased institutional adoption and the growing use of its financial services will create that demand remains a key question for XRP holders.

#5208. Bitcoin Sentiment Can Turn Quickly, British Strategy CEO Says

Andrew Webley, CEO of The Smarter Web Company, said that Bitcoin's drop has been sharper than he had anticipated, but he does not think the digital asset's price will decline much further.

The British CEO, whose company recently added 55 BTC to its treasury, said investors' opinions on Bitcoin can shift considerably without any changes to Bitcoin itself.

"Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very quickly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley said on X.

Webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline shows investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

However, Bitcoin's performance relative to the broader market may indicate BTC is being sold specifically or whether investors are taking profits across multiple markets. Webley did not specify which assets he was comparing Bitcoin against.

"Do I expect Bitcoin to go significantly lower from here? No. But as the past few weeks have shown, predicting short-term price movements is a very challenging task," Webley said.

Some of the most challenging periods for investors, he said, were followed by some of his most profitable periods.

His most definitive prediction concerned Bitcoin's longer-term outlook: "Bitcoin has an incredible future."

In fact, Webley's company has been buying more Bitcoin as its price has been dropping.

On Nov. 17, Smarter Web said it spent around £2.75 million on 55 BTC, bringing its total holdings to 2,905 BTC.

The average purchase price was £49,991 per Bitcoin, roughly 38% below the treasury's overall average purchase price of £81,234 following the transaction.

Smarter Web borrowed around £2.6 million under its Coinbase credit facility to finance most of the purchase. The company used its existing Bitcoin holdings as collateral.

Following the transaction, Smarter Web had around £19 million outstanding under the dollar-denominated credit facility.

#5207. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

#5204. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

#5202. CZ Urges 1Password Users to Change All Their Passwords

After a hacker stole customer data, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao advised 1Password users to change all the passwords stored in the service.

1Password offered different advice about what users should do after the incident was disclosed on Nov. 25. The password management service said hackers hadn't gained access to the passwords stored in users' vaults, so there was no need to reset them.

"If you use 1Password, recommend you to change ALL your passwords. It's a pain in the neck, but necessary," Zhao said on X, replying to a post from Coin Bureau about the breach.

If you have a crypto exchange login stored in 1Password, this distinction is important.

1Password says hackers could access the email address a customer uses to log in to the service. But they couldn't see the exchange password saved in the customer's vault.

Scammers could still use the stolen email addresses to contact people they know are 1Password users.

1Password started investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting signs of possible unauthorized access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

From there, the hacker was able to steal private source code and inject malicious code into 1Password's backend services. The malicious code then downloaded certain administrative data about customers.

1Password publicly disclosed the breach on Nov. 25, six days later.

The company did not specify how many customers were affected or explain exactly how the hacker managed to take over the employee's account.

The stolen data included customer names, login email addresses, account and user IDs, and timestamps indicating account creation and last use.

The hacker also gained access to 1Password's software development and deployment systems.

1Password disabled the compromised employee's GitHub account and revoked the stolen access token.

The company also restored a clean version of the affected service and revoked or replaced potentially exposed internal credentials.

1Password also engaged independent security experts to review its response.

1Password recommends that customers check the 1Password app or type the company's website address directly into their browser if they receive an unexpected invitation or recovery message.

The company says it will never contact users to request their account password or Secret Key.

Update: 1Password claims that there is no need to change one's 1Password account password or any of the passwords saved in one's vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident.

Hi CZ! There’s no need to change your 1Password account password or any of the passwords you’ve saved in your vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident. We don’t store your account password or Secret Key, and getting into our backend systems didn’t give the attacker the keys to decrypt your vault. The attacker did copy account information for some customers, including names and email addresses, so we recommend watching for 1Password invitations or account recovery emails you weren’t expecting. You can read the full update on our blog: https://t.co/9fbzzAJr0B

#5200. XRP ETF Buyers Suddenly Return

U.S. spot exchange-traded funds for XRP recorded net inflows of $4.07 million on Nov. 25. XRP was the only cryptocurrency among the 10 ETF categories tracked in a SoSoValue snapshot shared by BankXRP to register net inflows.

Wednesday's inflows narrowed the net outflow gap for XRP ETFs. Following the latest inflows, XRP funds had recorded $21.25 million more in investor outflows than inflows over the 30 days ending Nov. 25.

That means the net outflows over the rest of the period totaled $25.32 million. In a single trading day, investors covered about 16% of that shortfall.

The five U.S. spot XRP ETFs tracked by SoSoValue currently have total net assets of $1.04 billion. This is marginally higher than the $1 billion held by nine spot Solana ETFs.

However, there is a larger disparity in cumulative net inflows between XRP and Solana funds. Cumulative net inflows total $1.79 billion for XRP and $1.51 billion for Solana.

The two figures measure different things. Cumulative net inflows represent the total amount of money invested in the funds minus redemptions.

Net assets, on the other hand, represent the current value of a fund's holdings. This figure changes with the price of XRP.

This explains why XRP funds have a little over $1 billion in net assets despite attracting nearly $1.8 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Trading activity was slightly higher in Solana ETFs on Wednesday, with total volume reaching $35.54 million, compared to $33.40 million for XRP.

However, Solana ETFs recorded zero net flows for the day.

Investors can trade existing ETF shares with one another without affecting the total amount of money invested in the funds.

The contrast with Bitcoin ETFs was stark.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $123.41 million in net outflows on Wednesday, according to preliminary figures reported by SoSoValue.

However, the total for Bitcoin was still being compiled when BankXRP shared the numbers. SoSoValue marked the XRP total as complete.

With U.S. markets closed for Thanksgiving, XRP ETF buyers have only one more trading day this week.

Trading resumes on U.S. equity markets on Friday, Nov. 27. However, the session will end early, with markets closing at 1 p.m. Eastern time.

#5199. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its new tracks.

The best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

Node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the new ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

#5198. Altcoin Market Loses $408 Billion As Memecoin Dominance Falls to 2%

The altcoin market has contracted sharply, losing about $408 billion in market capitalization since its September peak as declining investor interest and persistent selling pressure continue to weigh on the sector.

Notably, the memecoins have been among the hardest-hit assets, with their share of the total altcoin market falling sharply from 11% to 2%.

According to CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost, the altcoin market has lost approximately 34% of its value. The decline is reflected in the performance of assets listed on Binance, where the percentage of altcoins trading above their 200-day moving averages has plunged from 90% down to 19%.

Meanwhile, meme tokens have suffered an even deeper loss of investor interest as selling pressure continues to outweigh buying activity. Binance’s Cumulative Buy/Sell Volume Difference shows a $1.5 billion imbalance in favor of sellers, a trend that has persisted since October 2025.

This shift has significantly reduced the segment’s share of the broader market. During the memecoin frenzy in November 2024, these tokens accounted for 11% of total altcoin market capitalization.

Adding to the pressure, more than 207 crypto exploits were recorded during the first half of 2026, setting a new historical record. Combined with declining liquidity and increased volatility, these security concerns have further weakened altcoins’ appeal.

Despite the widespread weakness, some market participants believe the sector could eventually regain momentum if Bitcoin establishes a stronger price base.

Crypto enthusiast Michael van de Poppe argued that Bitcoin needs time to recover from its recent correction, suggesting that several weeks of consolidation could precede a decisive breakout. He is looking to buy below $59,000, identifying that level as a potential entry point ahead of a recovery toward $70,000-$72,000.

Additionally, the analyst suggested that a Bitcoin rebound could create opportunities across the altcoin market, highlighting VVV and NIGHT as two tokens that could experience breakouts during such a move.

Meanwhile, analyst “@el_crypto_prof” offered a more optimistic assessment of altcoins’ longer-term prospects.

Pointing to the OTHERS/BTC chart, which tracks smaller cryptocurrencies against Bitcoin, the analyst noted that it has remained relatively stable despite the recent market weakness. He believes the trend could eventually support an altcoin recovery and urged investors to remain patient.

#5197. How AI Might Break Crypto: Explaining P vs NP Problem

The P vs NP question in computer science pops up in our feeds way more often than it did just a few days ago. No wonder—it's a problem mostly relevant and interesting to mathematicians and computer scientists, and it's also a Clay Millennium Prize problem. It asks a relatively simple question: whether every problem whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly.

Short answer: no, it can't. P vs NP is an efficiency question. NP is about whether a proposed solution can be checked efficiently, while P covers problems that computers can solve efficiently. For example, solving a complicated Sudoku certainly takes time, but checking the result is not as hard.

The question itself simply asks whether every checkable problem has an efficient solution. P ≠ NP says that some problems are harder to solve than to verify, and that is a core question: most scientists expect P ≠ NP, but proving it is the hard part.

Cryptography is purely mathematical, so issues relevant to computation apply here. ZK-proofs represent a more relevant crypto technology used every day and connected to NP: a statement (such as a transaction) is proven without revealing additional data (a zero-knowledge proof).

But the question is different: could it raise any problems, cause security concerns, or lead to exploits? To some extent—yes. Public-key cryptography is certainly something that can be affected right away—as can blockchains, wallets, and even HTTPS—but P=NP alone wouldn't break the whole industry.

Not really, because you can't change the fundamental math. Even if consensus mechanisms are changed and networks are upgraded, it would be similar to solving 2=2. It's fundamental. But instead of 'solving' it, cryptocurrency projects might adapt to such challenges. New systems might avoid relying on assumptions, so such a change would be a reaction to the consequences.

Quantum computing is a different story. Unlike P vs NP, quantum computing is not just a theoretical question about computational complexity. It's a technological development that could directly affect existing cryptographic systems.

A Zcash (ZEC) whale that bought 23,412 ZEC nine years ago moved 15,750 ZEC worth $11.39 million after nine years of inactivity, Lookonchain reported on Thursday. According to Lookonchain, the whale paid $5.04 million for the coins at an average price of $215.

Lookonchain also said that after nine years of holding, the whale was finally selling, and that his total profit on the position was more than $12 million.

Arkham data shows that the whale sent the ZEC in two transactions. The first one, 8,000 ZEC worth $5.73 million, went to an address without an Arkham label. About an hour later, the wallet sent 7,750 ZEC worth $5.66 million to a Kraken deposit address.

The whale got the coins nine years ago from Zcash's shielded pool. He withdrew most of them in batches of 250 ZEC, according to Arkham.

On Thursday, Lookonchain also reported that another whale deposited about 47,500 ZEC, or $35.8 million, to Binance.

ZEC dropped as low as $675.67 over the past 24 hours and was trading at $748.87 on Thursday, according to CoinGecko. CoinGecko put the market capitalization of ZEC at $12.77 billion, which made it the 11th-largest cryptocurrency. On Nov. 18, the price of ZEC was around $927.

A day before that, BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes set a $1,800 target for ZEC with no deadline. Hayes put Zcash in a group of four tokens that he called the "Four Horsemen," together with Ethereum, NEAR and Venice Token.

"The Four Horsemen shall pump and then usher in the end of the AI bubble," Hayes wrote on X. According to Hayes, the size of his position is "small to medium as conviction is meh."

Bitwise filed an S-1 for a Zcash ETF on Nov. 17 as well. The filing shows that the fund would trade on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC and would not use staking or shielded transactions.

On Thursday, Zakura, the Zcash development team led by Sean Bowe and Dev Ojha, asked users to move their ZEC out of the Sapling pool. Zcash launched Sapling in October 2018, and according to Zakura, about 400,000 ZEC still sits in it.

On Nov. 18, 2020, the Canopy upgrade at block 1,046,400 stopped new deposits into Sprout, Zcash's first shielded pool, according to the Electric Coin Company. Zcash activated its latest upgrade, NU7, at block 3,543,405 on Nov. 6. According to ZIP 218, NU7 cut the target block time from 75 seconds to 25 seconds.

"Practical pairing breaks are highly speculative," Zakura wrote about the cryptography behind Sapling.

#5194. NEAR’s Inflation Cut: The Math Behind a 5.27% to 3.37% Staking Yield

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. The cap formula, the epoch step and the yield math show what that does to stakers.

Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number. They earn about 5.27% today and will earn roughly 3.37% once the cut finishes, and a single line of arithmetic accounts for the gap.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto. The proposal touches one parameter, the maximum annual issuance rate, which drops from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. It is the second cut in just over a year, coming after the October 2025 halving from 5%.

Everything else stays put. Issuance still splits 90% to staking participants and 10% to the protocol treasury. There is no new spending program, no validator subsidy and no automatic trigger that could push issuance back up. The full proposal models 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided over two years and 66.1 million over six, measured against leaving the cap at 2.5%.

The schedule is a straight line with no stair steps:

Here t is the number of months since the reduction begins. The 0.9% is the total drop (2.5 minus 1.6), and dividing it by 24 gives a monthly step of 0.0375 percentage points, or 3.75 basis points. The min(t, 24) term caps the ramp at month 24, and the cap sits at 1.6% from there on.

NEAR applies the step every epoch rather than once a month. An epoch lasts about 12 hours, so the cap slips by roughly 0.0006 percentage points each time, far too little to notice on any given day. There are no step dates to mark on a calendar. Sampled every six months, the line looks like this:

The yield column uses the math in the next section. It drops about 0.08 percentage points a month, evenly, with no cliff.

New tokens go mostly to stakers, so the staked pool splits the reward, and a smaller pool earns more per token. That gives a working formula:

gross yield ≈ 0.9 × issuance cap ÷ staking ratio

The 0.9 is the staker share of issuance. Using the proposal’s figures, 0.9 × 2.5% ÷ 0.4271 comes to 5.27%, where 42.71% is the staking ratio reported when the proposal went to vote. Put in the 1.6% cap and 0.9 × 1.6% ÷ 0.4271 gives 3.37%, the same number the proposal publishes. Anyone can check the headline yields on a calculator.

The formula has two limits. It uses the cap, but realized issuance runs a little lower because transaction fees are burned. HSP-029 measured 2.45% in September, which puts today’s yield near 5.16%. The staking ratio also moves. When more people stake, the same rewards spread over more tokens and yield falls further, and when people unstake it climbs. The 3.37% figure assumes today’s ratio holds.

Stakers feel it first. By the proposal’s own math, someone staking 1,000 NEAR ends up with about 20 fewer tokens after two years than if the cap had stayed at 2.5%. The numbers back that up: yield averages about 4.32% across the ramp, roughly 0.95 points under today’s rate for two years.

Holders who don’t stake come out ahead. More than half of NEAR’s supply sits unstaked, and every new token dilutes those holdings. Trimming the cap by 0.9 percentage points trims that dilution by the same amount each year. Stakers give up some reward so that everyone else gives up less value.

Validators get an easier path than in 2025, when the halving cut staking rewards from about 9% to 4.75% in a single upgrade. Operators now have 24 months to plan. NEAR’s analysis finds that most validator revenue comes from commission on delegated stake, so service quality and fee competition shape income more than the issuance rate does.

Recent history explains the setup. When the 2025 halving shipped, an earlier community poll had missed the two-thirds threshold, and critics said the core team pushed the change through anyway. HSP-029 sidesteps that argument by design.

Two separate approvals are required. Token holders voting through veNEAR set the direction, and that vote closed November 2 with 99.96% in favor and none against. Validators then decide on their own whether to adopt the protocol upgrade that makes the cap binding. The author, Sal Ternullo of SVRN, opened discussion on October 7, and the process ran through the Screening Committee and Security Council in public. Raising issuance again would take a new proposal and another round of validator adoption, so nothing can be added quietly later.

Ratification does not change issuance yet. A one-quarter grace period comes first, giving wallets, exchanges, custodians and staking providers time to update their disclosures. NEAR One then releases the upgrade and validators choose whether to adopt it, with the reduction starting about a quarter after ratification. On schedule, that means a start in early 2027 and a 1.6% cap around early 2029.

Three things are worth tracking. Validator adoption of the upgrade comes first, because the cap stays at 2.5% until enough validators run it. The staking ratio comes next, since it moves yield regardless of the formula. Last are the quarterly transparency reports NEAR has promised, which compare realized issuance with the schedule.

Price is a separate question. Lower issuance eases supply pressure, but nothing in it creates demand. The cap will follow its published line down, and yield will follow the cap.

#5193. New Bitcoin Core Update: Breaking Down the Details

The key reason behind the setup is error handling in a way where there's no break in wallet usage that needs manual intervention in the process, to a significant degree. Indeed, a Bitcoin wallet migration change was, broadly speaking, merged on November 25 by Bitcoin Core.

The pull request follows two earlier fixes, one for unnamed legacy wallets and another for crashes when Bitcoin Core couldn't write to the wallet directory, on the whole. In fact, the thinking is to handle failures in a controlled way so the process can (to some degree) automatically restore the original wallet without needing manual intervention.

This isn't the first fix for wallet migration either, in the actual application.

Some mismatches during wallet creation could crash the graphical app or cause it to return a generic error. Those differences are now caught by Bitcoin Core and reported, which lets the migration process restore the original wallet from its backup, There are a couple of cases where the process could abruptly stop.

Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory could also throw an error and skip cleanup, in real-world scenarios. In fact, now the process crashes with a clear error message. The test for this case is checking that the wallet is still in the old database format after the failure.

The biggest change is in how Bitcoin Core moves the wallet to SQLite. Earlier, it deleted the original database before writing the new one. If something went wrong while making the new database or writing the wallet records, the user could end up restoring the backup by hand.

Now Bitcoin Core builds the SQLite database next to the original. So, the old database stays in place. These days, the new one is being built. Once the wallet records have been written successfully, Bitcoin Core can move the new database into place. The pull request also tests this with a wallet stored on a separate filesystem.

A leftover SQLite journal in the wallet directory can corrupt the new database if SQLite uses it for the migrated wallet. In fact, Bitcoin Core now stops the migration when it finds a file, and the test checks that the journal stays in place. Moreover, the wallet keeps its legacy format.

It's significant to keep in mind that automatic recovery still hinges on the backup being copied back successfully. As Ryan Ofsky mentioned in his review, if that copy crashes, the user still has to restore the backup by hand, on the whole.

Coinbase has suspended trading for 12 crypto trading pairs, including those of Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM), as November 2026 wraps up with just a few days left.

The delisting took place on November 25, as Coinbase announced earlier. The affected pairs include APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, XLM-BTC, ICP-BTC, and ADA-ETH, among others.

The full list includes APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, and SNX-GBP, with trading suspended across Coinbase Exchange, Advanced Trade and Coinbase Prime.

Coinbase regularly monitors the markets on the exchange and, in an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, has removed a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

In similar delisting news, Coinbase has disabled trading for Stargate Finance (STG), Vulcan Forged (PYR), Neon EVM (NEON), and Syndicate (SYND), in line with the shake-up on its platform in November. Users' funds will remain accessible, and users will be able to withdraw them at any time.

As stated earlier, Coinbase regularly monitors the markets on the exchange and might delist some assets to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity.

Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Centrifuge (CFG) on December 18, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Centrifuge has separately announced it is ending token support for CFG and allowing holders to convert CFG tokens into equity in Centrifuge.

Also in December, Coinbase will be performing a system upgrade. In an X post, the exchange stated it has scheduled a system upgrade for Saturday, December 5, 2026, around 7 a.m. PT, estimated to last about 4 hours.

During this time, Coinbase stated that all trading and transfers will be unavailable, and the Coinbase Exchange will be temporarily offline. Users are advised to take note and prepare accordingly so as to avoid any delays on that date.

Two XRP Ledger lending amendments, LendingProtocol and LendingProtocolV1_1, each have 28 votes out of 35 validators, or 80%, according to XRPScan data on Thursday. Each of them needs one more vote to start a 14-day countdown to activation, according to XRPScan.

On Wednesday, the SingleAssetVault amendment reached 29 votes. According to XRPScan, its earliest activation date is Dec. 9, and its support has to stay above 80% until then.

XRP was trading at around $0.95 on Thursday, up 4.1% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap.

On Nov. 20, XRPScan showed 25 votes for SingleAssetVault and 24 votes for each of the two lending amendments. Validators run by Interledger, onXRP, GateHub and Flare were among the last to vote for them.

RippleX opened LendingProtocolV1_1 for voting with a post on X on Sept. 30, when the amendment arrived with rippled version 3.4.0. "LendingProtocolV1_1 is open for validator voting. It introduces closed-ended vaults and cash-basis accounting for XRPL lending, and it must activate before LendingProtocol and SingleAssetVault can proceed," the RippleX developer account wrote.

J. Ayo Akinyele, head of engineering at RippleX, explained the role of the update in a post on June 25. "v1.1 is an enhancement to the Lending Protocol, not a replacement for v1.0," he wrote, adding that "Lending on XRPL will evolve dynamically."

Ripple described the mechanics of the protocol on Nov. 19. "The upcoming XRP Ledger Lending Protocol is designed to bring loan issuance and repayment directly onto the ledger. Lenders deposit into a Single Asset Vault, and the Lending Protocol lets loan brokers use that capital to issue loans and track repayments onchain," the company wrote on X.

Ripple engineer Ed Hennis presented the protocol in a thread on X in December 2025. He called it a protocol-native system for "fixed-term, fixed-rate, underwritten credit." "XRP's $124B market cap can finally be lent into institutional credit facilities to generate real yield instead of sitting idle," Hennis wrote at the time.

Jazzi Cooper, head of product at RippleX, wrote on Sept. 11 that "XRP as collateral for institutional credit is a killer use case (and supported by xls65/66 lending protocol!)"

On the same day, the XRP Ledger Foundation shared an interview with its chief technology officer, Denis Angell. "We are writing TradFi primitives into the XRP Ledger," Angell said. In the interview, he compared the lending protocol to a closed-end fund, where investors put in XRP or RLUSD and receive interest.

The crypto markets have shown early signs of stabilization today, even as sentiment sits in extreme fear territory. The recovery has tracked gains in tech futures and commodities following the Thanksgiving holiday, with 24-hour crypto liquidations totaling $228.95 million (mostly in short positions) and open interest at $272.6 billion.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded their largest monthly outflow on record, but BTC’s price bounce alongside broader risk assets points to resilience after recent volatility. The underlying strength in Bitcoin has also arrived as developers push forward with Layer 2 networks aimed at improving BTC’s transaction speed and expanding its practical uses.

This week’s most prominent BTC Layer 2 project, Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER), has finished its public presale campaign after raising $33.3 million. Buyers are now able to claim the HYPER tokens they purchased, and the token has been listed on Uniswap and Raydium. This project’s completed raise and progress toward a functional Layer 2 network position it to play a major role in Bitcoin’s evolution as the mainnet approaches.

Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER) is building a completely new Layer 2 network that processes transactions off Bitcoin’s main chain while anchoring final settlement back to the Layer 1. The L2 runs high-throughput operations through the SVM (Solana Virtual Machine), allowing near-instant finality for payments, DeFi activity, and decentralized applications.

Users will need to deposit native BTC to a monitored address; a smart contract then verifies the deposit against Bitcoin headers and proofs before minting an equivalent amount on the Layer 2. Batches of activity are compressed, protected by zero-knowledge proofs, and periodically committed to Bitcoin for security.

HYPER is the native token of the new L2, has a fixed supply of 21 billion, and functions as the gas token for fees on the network. Holders can also stake it to earn high-APY rewards. On the tokenomics side, allocations are 30% for development, 15% for rewards, 25% for the project’s treasury, 20% for marketing, and 10% for listings.

Audits by Coinsult and Spywolf (covering the HYPER token contract) and Hacken (covering L2 components) have also been completed.

Presale participants can now claim their HYPER tokens by first hard-refreshing the official Bitcoin Hyper site to clear the cache, then connecting the same wallet used for the original purchase. From there, they can choose either to claim the tokens directly or to claim and stake them at the same time.

Purchases made with Solana will be claimed on the Solana blockchain, while those completed with Ethereum, BNB, or a credit card can be claimed on Ethereum (contract addresses are specified on the official Bitcoin Hyper website). Once received, the tokens can be exchanged on Uniswap and Raydium.

Tokens that were staked during the presale become claimable starting December 3, and that date also marks the scheduled activation of the Layer 2 mainnet, which will include a dedicated wallet, transaction explorer, and bridge.

#5188. Sam Bankman-Fried Eyes Possible Return to Crypto, AI and Finance After Prison

Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried would consider a return to crypto and philanthropy after his time in prison, while weighing the impact on his reputation. The embattled digital asset executive was sentenced after an infamous collapse that plunged the sector into murky waters.

In an interview with Eli Goldfine, SBF discussed possible options after his release amid the negative impact on his reputation. He might make a crypto return despite this past run with the collapsed crypto exchange, FTX.

SBF said he would consider it depending on when and how he got out, and he also commented on the criminal justice system. His return to finance and crypto is to resume earning money for charitable donations and other causes.

“I would strongly consider it. It would depend on when I got out and how. I’d strongly consider crypto, AI, and finance more generally… “I think Anthropic is clearly one of, if not the top, AI companies,” he said.

Previously, SBF was big on donations through the concept of earning to give, urging wealthy founders to direct a portion of their earnings to charity. Though in jail, SBF is keen on artificial intelligence and its impact on finance and technology.

Per the interview, he tipped small companies built around AI products scaling between $100 million and $1 billion within years. This follows the ongoing AI wave attracting billions from traditional investors, underscoring capital rotation from other sectors.

Anthropic’s IPO has led to funds circling the market, with whales targeting new highs in related stocks. Meanwhile, crypto products have suffered, with asset prices falling to multi-month lows.

Furthermore, SBF warned against companies positioning as pro-AI just to attract funding. Recall that SBF backed Anthropic through Alameda Research, investing $500 million before selling its entire holdings in 2024 to pay debts.

While he planned his return after his sentence, SBF admitted his role in public discourse might be limited because of his current reputation. “…looking at public discourse, politics, and media, I’m not sure what role I could play, if any. But earning to give is a default.”

FTX collapsed in 2022, fueling a massive selloff and billions in losses. The aftermath led to tighter regulations and a lengthy investigation of executives linked to the exchange.

#5187. XRP Exchange Outflows Hit 5 Billion as Price Rebounds

XRP has seen traders withdraw large amounts of tokens out of major crypto exchanges, especially Binance, over the last 30 days even as the broad market volatility persists.

Despite the intense selling pressure XRP has witnessed over the past few months, data from the crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant shows that XRP’s exchange outflow has reached 5 billion XRP over the last month.

While the massive 30-day exchange outflow of 5 billion XRP is a relief signal because it signals persistent demand for XRP even amid the intense volatility, further data shows that the outflow is relatively low compared to levels seen in October.

Although the 5 billion XRP outflow is significant and November has yet to wrap up, the data shows that it marks a decent decrease from October, when total exchange outflows for the month reached about 5.7 billion XRP.

Despite the 700,000 XRP decrease in the metric, the outflows registered in the last 30 days are still considered substantial and have drawn attention from market analysts as they signal strong investor conviction even as XRP suffered larger price losses this month compared with October.

Usually, increases in the exchange outflow of an asset suggest that investors are moving assets off exchanges into external wallets, most likely to hold them for longer periods.

Hence, this metric provides a bullish signal for XRP as it indicates strong demand among traders, putting Binance in the spotlight as over a billion XRP were withdrawn from the exchange during the period.

While OKX and Bybit saw traders withdraw 865.27 million XRP and 697.65 million XRP from their platforms, respectively, Binance registered the highest XRP withdrawals, with about 1.439 billion XRP leaving its exchange over the period.

#5186. Why Does AI Get Simple Questions Wrong? What Google's Humanity's First Exam Shows

You ask an AI model to name the color of the third letter in each word on a neon sign. It gets it right. You ask again, and it slips by one letter. Nothing broke.

The model could do the task. It just did not do it every time. Google DeepMind built a test for exactly that gap, and the results show how far "usually right" can sit from "reliably right."

Most AI benchmarks ask a model to solve a hard problem once. If it passes, it scores. Google DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam (HFE), released on November 24, 2026, asks something different. Can a model solve an easy task, and slight rewrites of it, every single time?

The prompts are elementary on purpose. They cover counting objects, naming colors, tracking where something moved, basic arithmetic, strict formatting rules and spotting false premises. Humans solve them in about a minute.

One public example: "List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon." The answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue.

The paper calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap. One slip anywhere in the 16 answers fails the whole family.

The top five models score 96% to 98% on a single try and 100% on family pass@4. Their family pass⁴ averages only 85.8%. Across all 18 models, the gap runs from 7.6 to 80.1 percentage points.

The bottom row is the sharpest case. That model gets 68.7% of single tries right, yet clears only 18.6% of question families every time. Its family pass@4 is 98.8%, so it could solve nearly every family at least once.

The math is simple. Say a model is right 90% of the time on each answer, and the answers are independent. Getting 16 in a row right happens about 18.5% of the time (0.9 to the 16th power). That is a rough illustration, not the paper's calculation, but it shows how small error rates compound.

The paper's own example makes the same point. One model trails the leader by 6.6 points on single tries and by 29.4 points on family pass⁴. On average, about half the shortfall comes from prompts a model always fails. The other half comes from flakiness: right on some runs, wrong on others.

Humans and models also struggle in opposite places. People were least accurate on math and logic seeds. Models were strongest there and weakest on counting and reading text inside images.

Traders now hand AI tools real jobs: reading a contract, summarizing a token page, checking a wallet address in a screenshot, or running a bot. In those jobs, one wrong character or one miscounted number is the whole failure. A model that is right 19 times out of 20 will still be wrong on the 20th, and a signed transaction cannot be undone.

1. Ask twice. Run the same question more than once. If the answers differ, treat both as unconfirmed.

2. Check the visual parts yourself. Counts, colors, positions and text read from an image are where models slip most. Compare addresses and numbers character by character against the original.

3. Match the effort to the task. More reasoning helps with text and math. It helps little with images, so do not assume a longer "thinking" mode makes a screenshot read safe.

4. Keep a human on irreversible steps. Sending funds, signing transactions and changing settings should not rest on a single AI answer.

Shiba Inu's (SHIB) market structure remains bearish. SHIB trades near $0.00000365 on November 26. Its daily chart is showing selling pressure, with no validated reversal. Therefore, realistic recovery scenarios are largely tied to a general market retracement rather than local developments.

Shiba Inu quite often follows general market trends, despite seeming like a memecoin leader. The illiquid market always creates certain issues for assets like Shiba Inu. Apart from poor liquidity, another major factor is the lack of inflows into these assets.

Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and other larger assets have been printing outflows throughout November. When larger assets do not attract enough capital, SHIB and smaller assets almost always witness outflows or passive positioning among investors.

Despite mixed on-chain signals, the bearish trend may persist. Shiba Inu is already oversold, and conditions might become even worse.

Meanwhile, SHIB is approaching oversold territory and remains below declining moving averages. This could allow for a bounce, but oversold conditions do not guarantee a market bottom.

Taken together, the data presents a constructive on-chain backdrop: exchange-held supply is shrinking while short-term holder profitability is recovering. The key question for the next phase is whether reserves continue falling as BTC moves higher, or whether a stronger rally encourages previously withdrawn coins to return to exchanges and increases available selling supply.

As the total number of burn transactions approaches the 22,000 mark, Shiba Inu’s token-burning activity is nearing another significant milestone.

The number of SHIB burn transactions currently stands at 21,991, with only nine transactions to go to reach the 22,000 milestone, according to Shibburn. In total, these transactions have burned 410,845,372,884,899 SHIB.

This is a testament to the continuing efforts by the SHIB community to reduce the cryptocurrency’s massive circulating supply by sending tokens to unreachable wallet addresses. The tokens are sent to these dead wallets and are then permanently out of circulation.

Shiba Inu began with an initial supply of approximately one quadrillion tokens. Since then, over 410.8 trillion SHIB tokens have been burned, meaning that 41.08% of the original supply of 1 quadrillion tokens has been destroyed. But individual burns have very different effects. Some transactions are for relatively small amounts, while others remove millions or even billions of SHIB from circulation.

The milestone is another sign of the community’s ongoing interest in Shiba Inu’s tokenomics as investors look for developments that could create stronger demand across the ecosystem.

The daily burn rate of Shiba Inu has seen a huge spike of 443%, as the SHIB community continues its attempt to shrink the circulating supply of the cryptocurrency.

A higher burn rate indicates more tokens have been destroyed than on the previous day. According to Shibburn, 4.40 million SHIB have been burned in the last 24 hours, with the daily burn rate jumping 443%. This contributes to a total of 8.42 million SHIB burned in the last seven days and 322.85 million SHIB sent to dead wallets in the last 30 days.

Despite these cumulative burns, SHIB’s price performance still depends on broader market conditions and investor demand. At the time of writing, SHIB was up 5.60% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000364 amid the Thanksgiving holiday and down 6.45% weekly.

KuCoin will delist Monero (XMR) on Nov. 30, the exchange announced on Thursday. XMR dropped as low as $436 after the announcement and lost almost 15% within four hours, according to Kraken data on TradingView.

In the notice, KuCoin said that XMR would be delisted "in accordance with the Special Treatment Rules of KuCoin." The exchange closed XMR deposits on Thursday and will remove the XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC pairs at 08:00 UTC on Nov. 30.

KuCoin will also shut down XMR trading bots, Convert swaps and Earn products before the delisting. Users can withdraw XMR until Dec. 31, and KuCoin said that it could close withdrawals earlier if the Monero network stops producing blocks or processing transfers.

On Thursday, KuCoin's XMR/USDT pair had $73.8 million in 24-hour volume, according to CoinMarketCap. It was the largest Monero spot market and accounted for 47% of XMR spot trading. HTX's XMR/USDT pair was second with $29.5 million.

KuCoin did not mention its XMRUSDT perpetual contract in the notice. The contract had $33 million in 24-hour volume on Thursday, according to CoinMarketCap. Binance had the largest XMR perpetual market with $89.3 million.

PerpetualCow, who promotes the Wagyu trading platform on X, also responded to the delisting. "Over 50% of users sourced their XMR indirectly from KuCoin; it fuelled ALL instant swap exchanges," he wrote on Thursday. According to PerpetualCow, instant swap services "don't have their own liquidity" and "simply wrapped around KuCoin and sold/bought into their order books."

In the same post, he wrote that Wagyu had done more than $1.5 billion in volume in less than a year. He also shared a screenshot of Wagyu's XMR-USDC market together with the post, and it showed $63.5 million in 24-hour volume.

Earlier in November, the MEXC exchange also delisted XMR. The exchange removed XMR spot and perpetual markets on Nov. 13.

OKX delisted XMR in January 2024, and Binance removed the coin on Feb. 20, 2024. Binance said at the time that it would conduct a deeper review "when a coin or token no longer meets this standard, or the industry changes." XMR fell more than 15% after the Binance announcement.

Kraken stopped XMR trading for clients in the European Economic Area at the end of October 2024. In August 2025, Kraken announced an XMR delisting for Canadian clients "due to recent compliance requirements in Canada" and disabled trading for them on Sept. 2, 2025.

XMR fell more than 20% on November 26, briefly touching around $430 after KuCoin announced its delisting.

KuCoin will close four XMR spot markets on November 30, with withdrawals scheduled to remain open until December 31.

MEXC has also removed XMR spot and futures markets, while Eigenwallet's atomic swaps offer another exchange route.

Monero took a sharp hit on November 26, with the KuCoin Monero delisting announcement landing as XMR suffered its biggest single-day decline since June 4.

The timing is hard to ignore. But one exchange announcement doesn’t explain every sell order.

KuCoin confirmed it will close four XMR spot markets “XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC” at 08:00 UTC on November 30.

Other services face separate cutoffs. XMR Flexible Savings ends November 27 at 12:00 UTC, while Convert closes November 30 at 03:00 UTC. Trading bots stop at 06:00 UTC, followed by spot trading at 08:00 UTC.

Withdrawals are scheduled to remain available until December 31 at 08:00 UTC. Deposits are already closed. KuCoin says open orders will be cancelled when trading ends, while Flexible Savings balances and accrued earnings will move to Funding Accounts.

The exchange also warns withdrawals could be suspended earlier under certain project-related circumstances. It hasn’t provided a detailed reason for the removal.

KuCoin isn’t the only venue cutting Monero access. MEXC previously announced the removal of XMR spot pairs and later issued a separate notice covering XMR and DASH perpetual futures.

Those are different products. Spot markets provide access to the underlying asset, while perpetual contracts offer derivatives exposure.

Earlier Monero research from TRM Labs described liquidity becoming concentrated across fewer venues following exchange restrictions. That context matters, but it doesn’t establish how much of Thursday’s sell-off came from KuCoin.

Monero’s official account also announced an Eigenwallet release supporting Bitcoin and Monero, including native atomic swaps. These swaps allow users to exchange the assets without depositing both with a conventional exchange.

Still, a new trading route doesn’t automatically replace the depth of removed order books. The KuCoin Monero delisting leaves XMR facing a practical liquidity question as the deadlines approach.

#5179. API3 Overhauls Its Token, Governance and Mission: A Fixed 200,000,000 Supply and a New Direction in AI

Disclaimer: The below article is sponsored, and the views in it do not represent those of ZyCrypto. Readers should conduct independent research before taking any actions related to the project mentioned in this piece. This article should not be regarded as investment advice.

In a single proposal executed on 4 November, API3 permanently capped supply, ended emissions, moved to one-token-one-vote governance, and removed its own ability to mint tokens, while pointing its signed-data infrastructure at the fast-growing economy of AI agents.

API3, a provider of first-party data infrastructure, has executed a proposal that resets the protocol on three fronts at once: its token, its governance, and its mission. The proposal permanently capped API3’s supply at 200,000,000, ended five years of token emissions, moved governance to a simpler one-token-one-vote model, and removed the protocol’s ability to ever mint new tokens. Together, the changes clear the ground for a sharper focus on bringing signed, verifiable data to decentralized finance and to AI agents.

Since 2021, API3’s staking pool has minted about 90.1 million tokens, roughly 47% of today’s supply, at a pace near 950,000 a week, or close to 26% a year. The proposal minted API3 one final time to reach exactly 200,000,000, removed every minter, and transferred ownership of the token contract to a dead address that no one controls. No new API3 can ever be created, and the token’s maximum supply, listed until then as effectively unlimited, is fixed and final.

SIMPLER GOVERNANCE, A SMALLER ATTACK SURFACE

Governance moves from the framework API3 built in 2021 to a streamlined model on Snapshot. Each API3 token counts as one vote, whether it is staked or simply held, and the DAO’s multisignature wallets execute what passes. Retiring the old contracts and ending the token’s mintability also closes a specific risk: a hostile vote reaching the mintable token contract and printing new supply.

Hostile votes have drained treasuries across DeFi, and an unlimited mint was the bigger prize. With no minter to capture and no owner to compromise, that path is removed. The change comes as the cost of finding smart-contract exploits falls sharply, making old, rarely touched code a standing target.

With its foundations settled, API3 is concentrating on where its five years of API and DeFi experience applies next. Its curation business runs on-chain lending markets on the price feeds it builds across Ethereum, Base and Robinhood Chain, backing them with its own treasury capital alongside outside depositors, a structure it calls skin in the game.

AirnodeHub, now live in early access at airnodehub.api3.org, extends API3’s provider-signed model to the wider API market, letting AI agents discover, verify, and pay original providers for signed data. As agents become a growing share of internet traffic and begin paying for data per call, API3 is positioning AirnodeHub as the place that work is sourced and paid for.

Revenue from API3’s live operations, its curation business and the activity behind it, already buys API3 on the open market every month. AirnodeHub does not yet earn revenue; once per-request payments go live, it is designed to add to those buybacks as well. With emissions ended and supply fixed, the token is built to be deflationary over time: a capped asset with recurring, revenue-funded buy-side demand in place of a steady flow of newly minted tokens.

API3 builds data infrastructure that delivers signed, real-world data directly from the providers that produce it. It runs first-party data feeds across DeFi, curates on-chain lending markets on those feeds, and is extending its provider-signed model to the wider API market through AirnodeHub. API3 is governed by its token holders through the API3 DAO, with a fixed supply of 200,000,000. The project’s broader work and the marketplace itself can be explored at api3.org and airnodehub.api3.org.
